title: How we know this
hookLine: the stories of this century come down through later Sikh chroniclers, Persian records and family memory

lines: A STORY COMES DOWN BY A ROAD.
NOT WHAT HAPPENED, BUT HOW WE KNOW.
cards: Listen back over the last few weeks on this path and count how often you heard two words: tradition says. Tradition says a brick struck the invader. Tradition says thirty stood.
Tradition says the mothers recited the hymns while they ground the grain. Those two words have been doing quiet work all along. They signal that a story has come down by a particular road.
So today, a different kind of lesson: not what happened, but how we know this.

teach.b: There are three main roads. The first is the Sikh chroniclers. Long tellings of this century were written down by Sikhs, some well after the events, from what their families and elders had told them.
They wrote as insiders, with love and grief, and kept names and places other records leave out. Tomorrow you'll meet one of them. The second road is the Persian records.
The courts and governors of the time kept histories in Persian, and so did some writers who traveled with the invading armies.

teach.h: PERSIAN RECORDS FROM THE OTHER SIDE.
teach.b: They wrote from the other side, some with contempt, calling the Sikhs rebels. But they sometimes confirm that a battle happened or a city fell, even while telling it their own way. The third road is memory.

Families who passed stories down. Places like the bunga by the Akal Takht and the gurdwaras of Delhi, which hold a story in stone. And the Ardas, which carries the martyrs into the congregations that say it.
Each road has its strengths and blind spots. Insiders remember what mattered to them; outsiders record what mattered to theirs. Memory keeps the heart of a story and sometimes rounds off its numbers.
So when historians set the roads side by side, they find places where all three agree, and places where they don't.

teach.h: SETTING THE ROADS SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: That's why this path says tradition says. It isn't a sneer, and it isn't a verdict. It's an honest label for how a story arrived.

how: Historians of the Sikh eighteenth century read Sikh chronicles, Persian court histories and oral tradition side by side; in gurdwaras, the same history is carried by the Ardas and by talks called katha.

o: a holy legend that should never be questioned
a family tree kept by village record-keepers
history, the story of the past and how it came down

games.q: the roads a story comes by — tap the pairs.
p: a sign of how a story reached us

s: every story of this century was written down as it happened
some Sikh chroniclers wrote well after, from what elders told them.
Persian writers sometimes confirm a battle even while telling it their own way
they wrote from the other side, but can agree that something happened.
saying tradition says means the path thinks the story is false
it labels the road a story came by, without ruling on it.

games.q: you're reading about one battle. a Sikh chronicle and a Persian history tell it differently. what do you do?
o: trust the Sikh chronicle and ignore the other.
set them side by side and note where they agree and differ.
trust the Persian one because it's older.
games.why: historians set the roads side by side. where they agree, the ground is firmer. where they differ, they say so.

practice: Bring to mind someone older who carries a story you only half know, a grandparent, an old neighbor, someone at your gurdwara, church or mosque, and wonder what they saw that you didn't.

Shape one simple question you'd like to ask them, what was it like when, who was there when, and hold the question and their face for the rest of the sit. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: itihas, history. Sikh chroniclers, Persian records, and memory kept in families, places and the Ardas: the three roads this story of the past has come down to us by. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for itihas, history, the Punjabi word for the story of the past.

carryVoice: Your line: how do we know. Asking where a story came from is a way of taking it seriously. See you tomorrow.
